title: GSAP and ScrollTrigger
description: Animate the web with GSAP: tweens, eases, and staggers, timelines that stay maintainable, then ScrollTrigger for scrubbed, pinned, scroll-driven scenes, parallax, and the batching, matchMedia, and reduced-motion work that keeps it fast and accessible. Every demo runs live in the lesson.

lessons.title: Your First Tween
lessons.content:
# Your First Tween **GSAP** (the GreenSock Animation Platform) animates anything with a numeric value: CSS properties, SVG attributes, canvas objects, plain JavaScript variables. It exists because CSS transitions run out of road quickly, sequencing, mid-flight control, scroll-linked playback, and cross-browser transform handling are all things GSAP does and CSS does not. ## The three core tweens A **tween** animates a set of targets from one state to another. - `gsap.to(targets, vars)`, animate *to* the values you give, from wherever the element currently is. - `gsap.from(targets, vars)`, animate *from* those values to the element's current CSS. This is the entrance-animation workhorse. - `gsap.fromTo(targets, fromVars, toVars)`, state both ends explicitly, for when you can't rely on the current values. Press **Preview** to run this, then edit the numbers and run it again: ```html

Edit the values below and hit Preview again.

``` - The first argument is a **target**: a CSS selector string, an element, an array, or a NodeList. A selector animates every match. - `x: 220` is GSAP shorthand for `transform: translateX(220px)`. Always prefer `x`/`y` over `left`/`top`: transforms are composited by the GPU and don't force the browser to recalculate layout on every frame. - `duration` is in **seconds**, not milliseconds. - `ease` shapes the motion over time. `power2.out` starts fast and settles, which reads as natural because real objects decelerate. ## Special properties Not every key in the `vars` object is a property to animate. These control the tween itself: ```html
``` - `delay` waits before starting; `repeat: 2` plays three times in total (the original plus two repeats); `repeat: -1` loops forever. - `yoyo: true` makes every other repetition run backwards, so the motion returns instead of snapping back. - `onStart`, `onUpdate`, `onComplete`, and `onRepeat` are callbacks. `onUpdate` fires every frame, so keep it cheap. > [!TIP] > A tween returns a Tween instance, so `const t = gsap.to(...)` gives you `t.pause()`, `t.play()`, `t.reverse()`, `t.progress(0.5)`, and `t.timeScale(2)`. Playback control like this is the main thing you give up by animating in pure CSS.

questions.prompt: Why does GSAP recommend animating x and y instead of left and top?
options: x and y compile to transforms, which are GPU-composited and don't force layout recalculation
x and y accept larger values
left and top cannot be animated by GSAP
questions.answer: x and y compile to transforms, which are GPU-composited and don't force layout recalculation

questions.prompt: In GSAP, the duration property is measured in milliseconds.
gsap.____() animates elements from the values you specify to their current CSS values, which makes it ideal for entrance animations.

lessons.title: Eases, Stagger, and Targets
lessons.content:
# Eases, Stagger, and Targets Two tweens with identical durations can feel completely different. The difference is the ease, and, when several elements move, the stagger. ## Eases An **ease** maps elapsed time to progress. GSAP's names combine a curve with a direction: - `power1` through `power4`, increasingly sharp acceleration. `power4.out` is dramatic; `power1.out` is subtle. - `.out` decelerates into the end, `.in` accelerates out of the start, `.inOut` does both. - `back.out(1.7)` overshoots and settles, good for things appearing. - `elastic.out(1, 0.3)` springs; `bounce.out` drops and bounces. - `none` (linear) for continuous motion like a marquee, where acceleration would look wrong. The rule that covers most cases: things **entering** use `.out`, things **leaving** use `.in`, and things moving between two on-screen states use `.inOut`. ```html
none
power2.out
back.out(1.7)
elastic.out(1,.3)
bounce.out
``` - `gsap.utils.toArray(selector)` converts any selector, NodeList, or array-like into a real array so you can `map`/`forEach` over it. - Each bar travels the same distance in the same time; only the ease differs. Watch how much personality that one string carries. ## Stagger When one tween targets many elements, `stagger` offsets their start times. ```html
``` - `stagger: 0.05` is the short form: each target starts 0.05s after the previous one. - The object form adds control: `from: 'start' | 'center' | 'end' | 'edges' | 'random'` or an index, `grid: [rows, cols]` for two-dimensional ripples, and `amount` to spread the *total* stagger over a fixed time regardless of how many elements there are. - `amount` is the safer choice for dynamic lists: `each: 0.05` over 200 items takes ten seconds, while `amount: 0.6` always finishes in the same window. > [!NOTE] > `gsap.from` with `opacity: 0` briefly shows the element at its final state before the first frame if the page renders slowly. Set the initial state in CSS (or with `gsap.set`) when that flash matters.

questions.prompt: Which ease is the conventional choice for an element entering the screen?
options: power2.out, because it decelerates into its final position
none, because linear motion is neutral
bounce.in, because it is the most noticeable
questions.answer: power2.out, because it decelerates into its final position

questions.prompt: stagger: { amount: 0.6 } spreads the total stagger across 0.6 seconds no matter how many elements there are.
gsap.utils.____() turns a selector or NodeList into a real array you can iterate.

lessons.title: Timelines
lessons.content:
# Timelines Sequencing tweens with `delay` values works until you change one duration and every later delay is wrong. A **timeline** is a container that positions tweens relative to each other, and it is the single most useful thing in GSAP. ## Building a sequence ```html

Kodstigen

Timelines keep sequences honest.

GSAP
``` - `gsap.timeline({ defaults })` applies those vars to every child tween, so you set `duration` and `ease` once. - Tweens added with no position parameter start when the previous one ends. That's the default and it's usually what you want. - The methods **chain**, because each returns the timeline. ## The position parameter The third argument of `.to()` / `.from()` places the tween on the timeline: | Value | Meaning | | --- | --- | | *(omitted)* | at the end of the timeline | | `'-=0.25'` | 0.25s before the end, an **overlap** | | `'+=0.5'` | 0.5s after the end, a gap | | `1.5` | at absolute time 1.5s | | `'<'` | at the *start* of the previous tween | | `'<0.1'` | 0.1s after the previous tween's start | | `'>'` | at the *end* of the previous tween | | `'myLabel'` | at a label added with `tl.addLabel('myLabel')` | Small overlaps (`'-=0.2'`) are what separate animation that feels designed from animation that feels like a list of steps. ## Controlling the whole sequence ```html
``` - A timeline exposes the same controls as a tween: `play`, `pause`, `reverse`, `restart`, `seek(time)`, `progress(0..1)`, `timeScale(n)`. - `progress()` is the hook that ScrollTrigger uses in the next lessons: scroll position in, timeline progress out. - Timelines nest. `masterTl.add(sectionTl)` composes a page-level sequence out of self-contained pieces, which is how real projects stay maintainable. > [!TIP] > Build long sequences with `tl.timeScale(4)` while developing so you're not waiting through the intro on every reload, then set it back to 1.

questions.prompt: What does the position parameter '-=0.3' do when adding a tween to a timeline?
options: Starts it 0.3 seconds before the end of the timeline, overlapping the previous tween
Starts it 0.3 seconds after the previous tween ends
questions.answer: Starts it 0.3 seconds before the end of the timeline, overlapping the previous tween

questions.prompt: A timeline's defaults object applies its values to every child tween added to that timeline.
Calling tl.____(0.5) jumps a timeline to its halfway point, and is the property ScrollTrigger drives when scrubbing.

lessons.title: ScrollTrigger Basics
lessons.content:
# ScrollTrigger Basics **ScrollTrigger** is a GSAP plugin that connects animations to scroll position. Register it once, then attach a `scrollTrigger` object to any tween or timeline. ``` ``` ## start, end, and markers The `start` and `end` strings each take two values: **"trigger-element-position scroller-position"**. `start: 'top 80%'` means "when the top of the trigger element reaches 80% down the viewport". Turn on `markers: true` while developing, it draws the four positions on screen and removes essentially all guesswork. Scroll the preview below: ```html
scroll down inside this frame

Fades in once

toggleActions: play none none none

keep scrolling

Plays and reverses

toggleActions: play none none reverse

and back up again
``` ## toggleActions `toggleActions` is four space-separated commands for four events, in this order: `onEnter onLeave onEnterBack onLeaveBack` Each is one of `play`, `pause`, `resume`, `reverse`, `restart`, `reset`, `complete`, `none`. The default is `'play none none none'`: it plays once on the way down and then stays put. - `'play none none reverse'`, plays going down, rewinds when you scroll back above it. The most common choice for section reveals. - `'restart pause resume reset'`, a fully re-playable element. ## once, and cleaning up - `once: true` kills the ScrollTrigger after it first fires, the cheapest option for one-shot entrance animations. - In a single-page app, call `ScrollTrigger.getAll().forEach(t => t.kill())` when unmounting a page, or use `gsap.context()` to scope and revert everything at once. Stale triggers pointing at removed DOM nodes are the number one ScrollTrigger bug. > [!WARNING] > Remove `markers: true` before shipping. They're rendered as real DOM elements and they will show up in production.

questions.prompt: What does start: 'top 85%' mean?
options: Fire when the top of the trigger element reaches 85% down the viewport
Fire when the page is 85% scrolled
Fire when 85% of the element is visible
Fire 85 pixels from the top of the element
questions.answer: Fire when the top of the trigger element reaches 85% down the viewport

questions.prompt: The four values in toggleActions correspond to onEnter, onLeave, onEnterBack, and onLeaveBack.
Setting ____: true on a ScrollTrigger draws labeled start/end indicators on screen while developing.

lessons.title: Scrubbing and Pinning

questions.prompt: Why should a scrubbed tween normally use ease: 'none'?
options: The scroll position already supplies the timing, so an extra ease decouples the motion from the user's scrolling
Other eases are not supported with scrub
questions.answer: The scroll position already supplies the timing, so an extra ease decouples the motion from the user's scrolling

questions.prompt: scrub: 1 adds about one second of smoothing so the animation catches up to the scrollbar instead of tracking it exactly.
An end value of '+=400' means the trigger ends 400 ____ of scrolling after the start.

lessons.title: Scroll-Driven Timelines and Parallax

questions.prompt: When a timeline is scrubbed by a ScrollTrigger, what do its tween durations control?
options: Only the relative proportions, since the whole timeline is stretched across the scroll range
The exact number of seconds each step takes
How many pixels of scrolling each step needs
questions.answer: Only the relative proportions, since the whole timeline is stretched across the scroll range

questions.prompt: invalidateOnRefresh: true makes ScrollTrigger re-evaluate function-based values when the viewport is resized.
Moving background layers less than the scroll distance and foreground layers more creates a ____ effect.

lessons.title: Responsive, Accessible, and Fast

questions.prompt: What does gsap.matchMedia() do that a plain window.matchMedia listener does not?
options: It automatically reverts the tweens and ScrollTriggers created inside it when the query stops matching
It makes animations run on the GPU
questions.answer: It automatically reverts the tweens and ScrollTriggers created inside it when the query stops matching

questions.prompt: When prefers-reduced-motion is set, it is fine to skip the reveal animation and leave the element at opacity 0.
Call ScrollTrigger.____() after anything changes the page height, so cached trigger positions are recalculated.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of ScrollTrigger.batch over one ScrollTrigger per card?
options: Elements entering in the same frame animate as one staggered group, with far fewer triggers to manage
It removes the need to register the plugin
questions.answer: Elements entering in the same frame animate as one staggered group, with far fewer triggers to manage

Inside a ScrollTrigger onUpdate callback, self.____ is 1 when scrolling down and -1 when scrolling up.

lessons.title: Final Project: An Animated Landing Page
lessons.content:
# Final Project: An Animated Landing Page

Build a single-page scroll experience that uses everything in this course, and that stays usable for someone who has motion sensitivity or a slow phone.

## Requirements

Build one HTML file (plus CSS and JS, inline or separate) with at least five full sections.

**1. Hero, on load**
- A GSAP timeline that reveals headline, subhead, and call-to-action with overlapping positions, not one after another.
- At least one `stagger`, and a deliberate ease choice per element you can justify.

**2. Section reveals, on scroll**
- Use `ScrollTrigger.batch` for a grid or list of at least eight items.
- Set the hidden state with `gsap.set` so nothing flashes before the first frame.
- Use `toggleActions` (or `once: true`) deliberately, and say why in a comment.

**3. A pinned, scrubbed scene**
- Pin one section and drive a timeline with `scrub`, at least three choreographed steps.
- Tune `end` so the section holds for a sensible distance on both a laptop and a phone.

**4. A scroll-linked detail**
- A progress bar, a counter, a parallax layer set, or a horizontal rail. One is enough, done well.

**5. Responsive and accessible**
- `gsap.matchMedia` with distinct desktop and mobile behaviour: mobile must do less, not the same thing scaled down.
- A `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` branch that sets final states and skips large movement, while keeping the page fully readable.
- Everything reachable and readable with JavaScript disabled, no content may depend on an animation to become visible.

**6. Performance**
- Animate only transforms and opacity in the scroll-linked work.
- No `markers: true` left in.
- Call `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` after web fonts load, or set explicit image dimensions so trigger positions are stable.

## Deliverables

1. The working page.
2. A short `NOTES.md`: your ease choices and why, where you chose overlap over sequence, what mobile does differently, and what you removed for reduced motion.
3. Evidence you tested at a narrow viewport and with reduced motion enabled, screenshots or a short screen recording.

## What good looks like

- The animation supports the reading order instead of competing with it; nothing important is hidden until it's scrolled to twice.
- Scrubbed motion uses `ease: 'none'`, entrances use `.out`.
- The reduced-motion version still feels finished, not stripped.
- Nothing shifts layout as it animates, and the page doesn't jank on a mid-range phone.

> [!TIP]
> Build the page with no animation first, and make it good. Animation added to a solid page reads as polish; animation used to distract from a weak page reads as noise.
